citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each
component and use based
positive meridians for all strands. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$
W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots
x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.
$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$
\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),
$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

citations.quote: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $D$ be a valid finite planar code for a regular diagram of $K$, choose a basepoint $b$ in the complement, and designate a starting under-arc. The finite procedure $\mathsf{Wirtinger}(D,a_0)$ terminates and returns a presentation with one positive-meridian generator for each under-arc and one crossing conjugacy relator for each crossing. For the based meridians determined by the diagram's common upper-collar paths from $b$, the homomorphism from the presented group to $\pi_1(S^3\setminus K,b)$ that sends each generator to its corresponding based positive meridian is an isomorphism. Changing the designated starting under-arc only relabels the same finite cyclic arc set and gives an isomorphic presentation. If all basing paths are changed by prepending the same based loop, every generator image is conjugated by the same element, so the isomorphism type is unchanged.

Assume full AC and use the standard oriented four-crossing figure-eight code of [[ex-knot-kt-01-worked-cases]], with its positive based under-arc meridians $x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4$ and compatible diagram access paths. Put $u=x_1$, $v=x_2$, and $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$. Then $$\pi_1(E_{4_1})=\langle u,v\mid vw=wu\rangle,$$ with $u$ a positive meridian. In this presentation $$X_3=uvu^{-1},\qquad X_4=v^{-1}uvu^{-1}v=w^{-1}v$$ are the old $x_3,x_4$. The preferred longitude based compatibly with $u$ is represented by $$\lambda=X_4u^{-1}vX_3^{-1}.$$ In particular its trace in any representation is the trace of this explicit word. The formula does not identify a zero-homology centralizing word as a longitude without the diagram-parallel calculation.

Let $A,B\in SL_2(\mathbb C)$ and put $a=\operatorname{tr}A$, $b=\operatorname{tr}B$, $c=\operatorname{tr}(AB)$. Every word matrix in $A^{\pm1},B^{\pm1}$ is a linear combination of $I,A,B,AB$ with coefficients in $\mathbb Z[a,b,c]$, computed by finite word induction. Consequently its trace is a polynomial in those three traces. If $a=b=x$ and $c=y$, the coefficients specialize to $\mathbb Z[x,y]$. The assertion includes scalar, unipotent, reducible and irreducible pairs and uses no choice axiom.

Assume full AC and let $G$ be a finitely presented group. Every regular function on $\operatorname{Hom}(G,SL_2(\mathbb C))$ invariant under simultaneous conjugation is a polynomial in finitely many word-trace functions $t_w(\rho)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(w))$. Equivalently, the coordinate algebra of the affine character quotient is generated by trace functions of words in $G$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the named suppliers. Let $G$ be a
complex reductive affine algebraic group and let $X$ be an affine algebraic set
with an algebraic $G$-action ([[def-rational-action-on-affine-variety]]). Then:
(i) $\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb C$-algebra; (ii) for any
finite generating set $f_1,\dots,f_n$ of $\mathbb C[X]^G$ the image of the
morphism $X\to\mathbb C^n$, $x\mapsto(f_1(x),\dots,f_n(x))$, is closed and is
canonically isomorphic to the affine variety with coordinate ring
$\mathbb C[X]^G$, so the quotient is independent of generators up to this
canonical isomorphism; (iii) the resulting surjective $G$-invariant morphism
$\pi:X\to X/\!/G:=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb C[X]^G$ is a categorical quotient
([[def-categorical-and-geometric-quotients-of-classical-varieties]]); (iv) for
every closed $G$-stable subset $Y\subseteq X$ the induced morphism
$Y/\!/G\to X/\!/G$ is a closed immersion, and for closed $G$-stable
$Y,Y'\subseteq X$ one has $\pi(Y\cap Y')=\pi(Y)\cap\pi(Y')$; (v) every fibre of
$\pi$ contains exactly one closed $G$-orbit; (vi) if $X$ is irreducible then so
is $X/\!/G$, and if in addition $X$ is normal then so is $X/\!/G$.

Assume full AC and let $K=J(2,-2)$ be the figure-eight knot. Use the two-bridge group presentation $\pi_1(E_K)=\langle u,v\mid v w=w u\rangle$, where $w=uv^{-1}u^{-1}v$, and take $\mu=u$. On the one-dimensional irreducible character component, define $x(\chi)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(u))=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(v))$ and $y(\chi)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(uv))$. Then
$$2x^2+y^2-x^2y-y-1=0,$$
and the preferred-longitude trace is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\lambda))=x^4-5x^2+2$. The displayed curve equation is irreducible over $\mathbb C$, and $x$ is nonconstant on it.

Assume full AC. Let $G=\pi_1(E_K)$ be the group of a smooth oriented knot exterior, with positive meridian $\mu$ and preferred longitude $\lambda$. For a finite presentation $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_n\mid r_1,\ldots,r_m\rangle$, the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ representation variety** is the algebraic set of tuples $(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in SL_2(\mathbb C)^n$ for which every relator matrix $r_j(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ equals the identity. The group $SL_2(\mathbb C)$ acts on this set by simultaneous conjugation. Its affine categorical quotient, whose coordinate ring is the invariant ring of regular functions, is the **$SL_2(\mathbb C)$ character variety** $X(E_K)$. For a representation $\rho$, its character is the function $\gamma\mapsto\operatorname{tr}(\rho(\gamma))$. A representation is **reducible** if its matrices preserve a common one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$; otherwise it is irreducible. The peripheral torus group is $\pi_1(T_K)\cong\mathbb Z^2$, generated by the meridian and preferred longitude; its image in $G$ is generated by their commuting classes and need not be isomorphic to $\mathbb Z^2$. Their image under any representation is a commuting pair of matrices, so it has a common invariant line and is simultaneously triangularizable over $\mathbb C$. Choosing a common invariant line gives meridian and longitude eigenvalues $(M,L)\in(\mathbb C^*)^2$; the unordered boundary character identifies $(M,L)$ with $(M^{-1},L^{-1})$. Simultaneous diagonalizability is stronger than simultaneous triangularizability.

Let $A,B\in M_2(\mathbb C)$ commute. There is a one-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb C^2$ invariant under both $A$ and $B$. Equivalently, in a basis beginning with a nonzero vector in that subspace, both matrices are upper triangular.

Let $k$ be a field and let $r\ge0$ be an integer. Then $k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ is a
unique factorisation domain ([[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]). Every
irreducible element of it is prime
([[def-irreducible-and-prime-elements-in-a-domain]]), and every prime ideal of
height one ([[def-height-of-a-prime-ideal]]) is generated by an irreducible
element.

For $r=0$ the ring is the field $k$ itself
([[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]]); it has no irreducibles and
no height-one primes.

Let $R$ be a unique factorisation domain and let $K=\operatorname{Frac}(R)$.

1. If $f,g\in R[x]$ are primitive, then $fg$ is primitive.
2. If $p\in R[x]$ is primitive and has positive degree, then $p$ is irreducible
   in $R[x]$ if and only if it is irreducible in $K[x]$.

Here a polynomial is **primitive** when its coefficients have no common nonunit
divisor.
